content.title: About
content.content: Cereal with peanut butter is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast consisting of whole grain flakes sweetened and coated with a smooth peanut butter spread. The product combines crunchy cereal with a rich nutty flavor, providing a quick source of energy and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter has been used in breakfast cereals for over 30 years.
The flakes are often fortified with B‑vitamins and iron.
The grain‑nut combination improves the bioavailability of certain minerals.
The product is packaged in convenient single‑serve bags for easy transport and storage.
In many countries similar cereals are sold under different brand names but with comparable formulations.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole grain flakes provide slowly digestible carbs that sustain energy levels for several hours.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter adds about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids from peanut butter promote heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortified cereals often include iron, zinc, vitamin B6 and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grains supply fiber that aids normal digestion.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: The product can trigger severe allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to peanuts.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugars, which may contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of cereal and butter makes the product energy‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added for flavor, which may be unsuitable for people monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cereal with peanut butter can be enjoyed dry, with milk or a plant‑based beverage, or mixed into yogurt, fruit, and nuts for a more filling breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the bag tightly to prevent moisture absorption and preserve crunchiness.

chili-hot-dog-sandwich-on-wheat-bun.title: Chili Hot Dog Sandwich on Wheat Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The Chili Hot Dog Sandwich is a warm handheld meal featuring a sausage smothered in spicy chili sauce, placed inside a soft wheat bun. The blend of heat, juicy sausage, and tender bread makes it a popular quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The chili‑and‑sausage combination originated in the United States in the early 20th century as street food.
A wheat bun gives a softer texture compared to the classic hot‑dog roll.
Spicy chili sauce is often made from fresh peppers, vinegar, sugar, and spices, giving it a distinctive aroma.
Chili hot dogs are frequently topped with mustard, ketchup, pickles, or onions.
Some regions use smoked sausages for a deeper flavor profile.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The sausage provides animal protein that supports muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat supplies iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausages contain vitamin B12 and niacin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in chili
items.content: Chili peppers are rich in vitamin C and capsaicin, which have antioxidant and thermogenic effects.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bun and fats from the sausage provide a quick source of calories.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages are often salty, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Fatty meat products may raise cholesterol levels when consumed frequently.

items.title: Spicy food irritation
items.content: Chili sauce can irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, which is unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: This quick snack is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, splitting the bun and adding chili sauce to taste. Optional toppings include mustard, ketchup, pickled vegetables, or cheese. Eat it right after preparation while the bun is still soft and the sauce aromatic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator, wrapped in plastic, for no more than 24 hours. Sausages and buns can be kept separately: sausages in an airtight container, buns in a dry place. Reheat in an oven or microwave before serving to avoid a soggy bun.

content.title: About
content.content: Cornmeal stick, Puerto Rican style are crunchy corn sticks made according to a traditional Puerto Rican recipe. A dough of cornmeal, water, salt and spices is shaped into thin sticks and fried until golden. They have a light corn aroma, a mildly salty flavor and a crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional recipe dates back to the early 20th century as a street snack in San Juan.
The cornmeal used is usually "masa harina," finely ground and often calcium‑enriched.
Sticks are commonly served with "mojo" or "mari" sauces – typical Puerto Rican tomato‑based sauces.
In Puerto Rico they are called "corn sticks" or "corn chips," but differ from American corn chips by having a softer interior.
They are a popular snack during festivals and carnivals.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Cornmeal provides slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When baked rather than deep‑fried, the sticks contain relatively little fat compared with many other snack foods.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn supplies dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and folate in corn aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Cornmeal is naturally gluten‑free, making the product suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: High salt levels can raise blood pressure; consume in moderation.

items.title: Calorie density when fried
items.content: Deep‑frying significantly increases the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sticks as a snack on their own, dip them in sauces (mojo, guacamole, salsa) or add them to salads for crunch. They are convenient for picnics, trips, and outdoor activities.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For storage longer than two weeks, keep refrigerated to maintain crispness and prevent mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried apricots are apricots that have had most of their water removed by sun-drying or dehydration, leaving a chewy, sweet-tart, concentrated fruit. They are eaten as a snack and used in baking, granola, stews, pilafs, and desserts. Some are dried with the pit (in Central Asia, whole dried apricots are called uryuk) and others are halved and pitted.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It takes several pounds of fresh apricots to make one pound of dried apricots.
Bright orange dried apricots are usually treated with sulfur dioxide, while unsulfured ones are darker brown.
Dried apricots have been a staple food in Central Asia and the Middle East for centuries because they keep for a long time.
Drying concentrates both nutrients and natural sugars.
They are widely used in both sweet and savory dishes, including pilafs and meat stews.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Dried apricots contain beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A for vision, skin, and immune function.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Dried apricots contribute fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Dried apricots contain iron, which supports oxygen transport.

items.title: Convenient energy
items.content: Dried apricots are a portable, long-lasting source of quick energy.

items.title: Sulfites
items.content: Sulfured dried apricots can trigger reactions in people with sulfite sensitivity or asthma. Choose unsulfured ones if you are sensitive.

items.title: Concentrated sugar and calories
items.content: Dried apricots are high in natural sugars and calories for their weight, so portions should be small.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Eating a lot of dried apricots may cause bloating or loose stools because of fiber and sorbitol.

items.title: Teeth and potassium
items.content: Sticky dried fruit can cling to teeth, and people with kidney problems or on certain medications should ask a healthcare professional about potassium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried apricots can be eaten as a snack, chopped into oatmeal, yogurt, granola, and salads, or cooked into pilafs, tagines, and stews. They can also be soaked in warm water to soften and used in baking and desserts. Eat a small handful at a time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried apricots in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, where they keep for several months, or in the refrigerator or freezer for longer storage. Keep them away from moisture. Discard dried apricots that show mold or smell fermented.

content.title: About
content.content: Frescavena is a plant‑based food product designed to support a healthy lifestyle. It has a mild flavor, light texture, and can be used in a variety of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frescavena is made from selected whole grains and legumes.
The product is gluten‑free and suitable for people with gluten intolerance.
It contains natural flavorings and minimal artificial additives.
Frescavena has a low glycemic index, making it suitable for blood‑sugar control.
Packaging is made from recyclable materials.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Provides high‑quality plant protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most of the fat is polyunsaturated, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B1, B2, B6 vitamins that are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Includes magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for nervous and immune systems.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the product’s components.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Excessive consumption may cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: The product contains a small amount of oxalates, which should be considered by people prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frescavena can be enjoyed as a snack, added to smoothies, porridge, yogurt, salads, or used in baking. It can also be soaked beforehand for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Frescavena in a sealed container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-dry-mix-made-with-wa.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, dry mix, made with water, with whipped cream

content.title: About
content.content: A dry mix for hot chocolate / cocoa is designed for quick preparation by simply adding hot water. The blend usually contains cocoa powder, sugar, powdered milk and flavorings. It is often topped with whipped cream, giving the drink a creamy texture and rich taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry mixes appeared in the early 20th century when cocoa powder began to be produced on an industrial scale.
In Russia, hot chocolate gained popularity after ready‑made mixes appeared in stores in the 1990s.
Whipped cream as a topping makes the drink more caloric but also more aromatic.
The cocoa powder used in mixes often undergoes Dutch processing, which removes most of the caffeine and theobromine.
Emulsifiers are sometimes added to help the cream stay on the surface.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa is rich in flavonoids that combat free radicals and support vascular health.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing
items.content: Caffeine and theobromine can boost serotonin levels and improve mood.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The mix typically provides magnesium, iron and calcium, important for muscles and bones.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Sugar and quick‑acting carbohydrates give an immediate energy lift, useful in cold weather.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Many mixes are fortified with vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which play roles in metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Adding whipped cream significantly raises the drink’s calorie count.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The mix often contains powdered milk, which may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or casein allergy.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: For caffeine‑sensitive individuals, drinking hot chocolate in the evening may disturb sleep.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 200‑250 ml of hot water over the mix, stir thoroughly until smooth, then add a dollop of whipped cream. You can garnish with grated chocolate, cinnamon or vanilla sugar. Serve hot in a mug.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3‑6 months. Store whipped cream separately in the refrigerator and add just before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Oat milk is a plant‑based beverage made from whole oat grains, water, and sometimes added ingredients (sweeteners, flavorings, vitamins). It has a mild creamy taste, a slightly sweet oat aroma, and a light‑cream color. Oat milk is suitable for vegans, people with lactose intolerance, and anyone looking for a dairy‑free alternative.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat milk gained popularity in Scandinavia in the early 1990s.
Oats contain beta‑glucans, which may help lower cholesterol levels.
Unlike many nut milks, oat milk typically contains no nuts, making it safe for most allergy sufferers.
Producing oat milk uses less water than producing cow’s milk.
Oat milk creates a stable foam, which is why it’s favored for coffee drinks.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans support healthy cholesterol levels and contribute to immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oat milk provides thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Oat milk fits well into diets that limit saturated fat intake.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber from oats can help maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Oats are often processed on shared equipment with wheat, so trace gluten may be present.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some brands sweeten their oat milk, increasing calorie content.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Oat milk can raise blood sugar levels more quickly than some other plant milks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Oat milk can be enjoyed on its own, added to coffee, tea, smoothies, cereals, baked goods, sauces, and soups. It is also used as a base for vegan desserts and ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store opened oat milk in the refrigerator for up to 5–7 days. Keep unopened cartons in a cool, dry place away from direct light.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese popcorn is a ready‑to‑eat snack made from puffed corn kernels coated with a savory cheese seasoning. It is popular as a quick bite at home, in the office, or on the go. The cheesy flavor comes from a blend of natural and artificial flavorings together with a small amount of vegetable fats that give it a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn originated in North America over 5,000 years ago, but the cheese‑flavored version became mass‑popular only in the late 20th century.
Cheese popcorn often contains microscopic particles of Parmesan or cheddar that create its distinctive aroma.
Unlike plain popcorn, the cheese version usually has a higher sodium and fat content.
When sealed in an airtight bag, cheese popcorn stays crisp for several weeks.
There are many cheese flavor variations, from mild melt to sharp cheddar.

items.title: Low calorie compared with many snacks
items.content: Air‑popped corn kernels are low in fat, so a serving of cheese popcorn typically contains fewer calories than chips or nuts.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Corn provides fiber that supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Corn contains polyphenols that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The carbohydrates in popcorn are rapidly digestible, giving a fast energy boost.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Corn supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese popcorn often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Some varieties use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain dairy, milk proteins, and flavorings that can trigger allergies.

items.title: Calorie density in large portions
items.content: While a single serving is modest, overeating quickly adds up in calories.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: To boost flavor, manufacturers often add artificial flavors and colorants that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese popcorn is convenient to eat straight from the bag as a snack while traveling, at work, or during a movie. It can also be sprinkled over salads for extra crunch or used as a topping for casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the popcorn in its original sealed bag in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to maintain crispness and flavor. Avoid moisture, as it will make the popcorn soggy.

potato-french-fries-from-fresh-baked.title: Potato, French Fries, from Fresh, Baked

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato fries are made from fresh potatoes cut into sticks and baked in the oven without excessive oil. They retain the natural potato flavor, have a crispy exterior and a soft interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked fries contain fewer calories than traditional deep‑fried versions.
Potato is one of the world’s most consumed vegetables, grown in over 100 countries.
Baking preserves more vitamins, especially vitamin C, compared with frying.
There are many seasoning options: paprika, garlic, rosemary, parmesan.
In Russia, “home‑made” oven fries are a popular side dish.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are high in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in fresh potatoes acts as an antioxidant and supports the immune system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Baked fries contain significantly less fat than deep‑fried ones, making them more diet‑friendly.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The skin of the potato provides dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high GI, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Excessive added salt to fries can increase the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Cooking at very high temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; bake at 200 °C and avoid over‑drying.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked fries are served as a side dish with meat, fish, or as a snack on their own. Sprinkle with favorite spices and dip in sauces such as ketchup, yogurt, or mustard. For extra crispness, pat the cut sticks dry and lightly coat with olive oil before baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked baked fries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in the oven to retain crispness. Raw potato sticks can be kept in cold water for up to 24 hours to prevent discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy nuts are roasted soybeans (Glycine max) that have a light nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. They are often used as an alternative snack for people avoiding traditional tree nuts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy nuts are made from soybeans, one of the most widely cultivated legume crops worldwide.
Unlike most nuts, soy nuts are not true nuts botanically; they are seeds of a legume.
In Asian cuisine, especially Japanese, boiled soybeans in the pod are called edamame, a close relative to roasted soy nuts.
Soy is rich in isoflavones, which can have phytoestrogenic effects.
Roasting enhances aroma but can also reduce some heat‑sensitive vitamins.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Soy nuts contain about 35 % protein, making them an excellent source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: They provide polyunsaturated fatty acids, including omega‑6 and a modest amount of omega‑3.

items.title: Source of B vitamins
items.content: Soy nuts supply B‑vitamins such as thiamine, riboflavin, and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: They contain iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and calcium, supporting bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Phytoestrogens
items.content: Soy isoflavones may help balance hormones, especially for women during menopause.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
items.content: Most soy worldwide is GMO; choose certified organic varieties if you wish to avoid GMOs.

items.title: High sodium in salted versions
items.content: Salted soy nuts can contain a lot of sodium, which is undesirable for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soy nuts can be eaten straight as a snack, tossed into salads, soups, rice or noodle dishes, and used in vegetarian and vegan recipes as a nut substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soy nuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
